In 1977, Dolly Parton invited her parents, Robert Lee and Avie Lee, and seven of her siblings onto her variety show to perform “In the Pines,” an old Appalachian folk song the family had sung together growing up in East Tennessee.

They performed several songs together that day, offering a rare glimpse behind Dolly’s enormous career. Before the records, awards and worldwide fame, music was something the Parton family shared at home — and watching them sing together shows exactly where so much of Dolly’s musical foundation began.

items.creator: technoandhousemusic
items.caption:
This is what the transition from the ’80s to the ’90s sounded like

On February 24, 1990, Technotronic brought “Pump Up the Jam” to Saturday Night Live and turned Studio 8H into a dancefloor.

The 1989 house/hip-house crossover had already become a global smash, reaching No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 2 in the UK. It also topped the US Dance Club chart.

Blending house, hip-hop and new beat, “Pump Up the Jam” became one of the defining crossover records of its era, helping bring club music to a massive mainstream audience.

Looking back, this performance feels like a time capsule of the moment dance music was breaking out of the clubs and into the mainstream.

The ’90s were about to sound very different.

When The Highwaymen first came together in 1985, they united four of country music’s biggest stars: #JohnnyCash, #WaylonJennings, #WillieNelson, and #KrisKristofferson. Their debut single, “Highwayman,” became an instant No. 1 hit and launched a hugely successful tour that introduced fans to one of the greatest supergroups in country music history.

Each member had already built a legendary solo career, but together they represented the rebellious spirit of outlaw country, earning the respect of both fans and fellow musicians while leaving behind one of the most iconic legacies in country music.

items.creator: chancemccoymusic
items.caption:
This was a gateway tune for me—one of the first ones I ever heard when I was starting to get interested in Bluegrass and old-time music.
•
After I got deeper into playing traditional folk, I kind of left this tune behind. I never really learned a definitive version; it was just a jam tune I’d occasionally play.
•
But like many traditional tunes, there was something much deeper waiting to be discovered behind this iconic folk melody. I decided to dive into Doc Watson’s version recently and boy, am I glad I did!
•
This is the way he played it on clawhammer banjo, and it absolutely blew my mind. His old-time playing is phenomenal—a driving, intricate melody full of pull-offs and drop-thumb at lightning speed in modal D-Dorian.
•
It was a revelation, and I wanted to know where he learned his version. Turns out the iconic minor melody we now associate with the tune was popularized by Jean Ritchie, who learned it directly from her father in Viper, Kentucky.
•
But that’s not the end of how deep this goes. This melody traces back at least 400 years and was recorded as Child Ballad #81, known as ‘Matty Groves.’ The kicker? The melody has stayed remarkably consistent for centuries.
•
So next time you go to play Shady Grove, think about that!
•
#oldtimemusic #clawhammerbanjo #docwatson #shadygrove americanfolklore

items.creator: chancemccoymusic
items.caption:
This 100-year-old tune was originally recorded in 1929 by a historic family string band called Crockett’s Kentucky Mountaineers. In a twist of fate, they became known as “California’s first country-music stars,” despite their authentic Appalachian roots.
•
John Harvey Crockett (1877-1972) was born into a fiddling family in West Virginia. He traveled by horseback and buggy through the mountains, teaching shape-note singing, banjo, and fiddle.
•
Around 1918, Dad Crockett packed his family into a Model T Ford (top speed: 40 mph!) and drove 2,300 miles from Sharpsburg, KY, to Fowler, CA. He worked as an auto mechanic until show business finally lured him away in 1927.
•
Once settled, John’s sons began performing on local radio. Johnny, known as a “cowboy balladist,” convinced his brothers and father to join him around the microphone, forming the Crockett Family Mountaineers.
•
They became a massive success, touring 47 states and landing a coast-to-coast CBS radio broadcast. In 1929, they cut a 78 RPM record titled “Medley of Old-Time Dance Tunes” for the Brunswick label.
•
“Sally in the Garden” appears on Part II (Brunswick 291). It stands out oddly as a minor modal tune among the common dance breakdowns.
•
There is also an amazing field recording of Marion Sumner playing this as a driving breakdown. It’s related to the ‘Hog-Eye Man’ tunes collected by Cecil Sharp and others in the Ozarks. Those verses show up in much older sea shanties, but the melody is different. Truly an ancient piece!
•
I don’t know who came up with this specific banjo version—the slow, haunting one I personally love so much. Maybe you know? Feel free to drop that, or any other tune lore, in the comments.
•
#ClawHammerBanjo #FolkMusic #Appalachia #MountainMusic #OldTime

items.creator: pop.music.culture
items.caption:
The khaen is a traditional bamboo instrument from Laos and northeastern Thailand. It’s made of multiple bamboo pipes connected to a small wooden mouthpiece, and each pipe produces a different note.

What makes it special is how you play it—you can both blow and breathe in to make sound. Inside the pipes are tiny metal reeds, so it actually works more like a harmonica than a flute. Because of this, players can create a continuous, flowing sound and even play simple chords.

The sound is warm and slightly buzzing, often with a steady, hypnotic feel. Traditionally it’s used in folk music and ceremonies, but nowadays people also use it in modern styles like electronic or ambient music—like the guy you showed.

🎥@jerem.khaen

Traditional Appalachian version of House of the Rising Sun. 🌅🪕

Did you know this was a traditional tune sung in the mountains? While the world knows the 6/8 rock version, the oldest recordings—like those from Roscoe Holcomb—carry this driving 4/4 rhythm. It feels less like a ballad from a bar and more like a dire warning from the hills.

While the world knows the 6/8 rock version, some of the oldest versions, like Roscoe Holcomb’s, carry this driving 4/4 rhythm that feels more like a dire warning from the hills than a ballad from the bar.

This 1800s-style banjo brings out the grit that has kept this melody alive for over a century.

Which version do you prefer? The old-time drive or the British Invasion swing? Let me know in the comments. 👇

items.creator: chancemccoymusic
items.caption:
Written in the 1930s, but still ringing true today. Which side are you on? Share this if you still believe the power belongs to the people, not the government.

I recorded this take live on the porch here at the Girardeau House. (More news about that coming soon!) I decided to keep the audio raw—crows and all—because some songs aren’t meant to be polished. They’re meant to be felt. The driving rhythm of the clawhammer banjo has always been the percussive heartbeat of the mountains, and “Which Side Are You On?” is a line in the sand that never fades.

This is the start of a new chapter. I’m heading back to my roots to find the music that actually matters in times like these.

What protest anthem is your favorite? Let’s talk in the comments. 👇

#FolkMusic #AppalachianMusic #ClawhammerBanjo #OldTimeMusic #BanjoPlayer

items.creator: gemsonvhs
items.caption:
John Prine & Iris DeMent - “In Spite of Ourselves”

	Today we’re looking back on a duet between two legendary figures of folk music. John Prine wrote this humorous track while recovering from radiation therapy and surgery on his throat. In a 2016 interview, he recounted requesting Iris Dement to join him on the track, “I kinda had her voice in mind when I was doing it because I know Iris can be a little sassy and she could tear this guy down… I told Iris, ‘I want you to listen to this and just see. It’s got a few questionable things in it that you’re gonna have to say. So you just tell me whether you would want to do it or not. We’ll leave it at that... So I didn’t hear from her for three weeks. Nothing. Finally, I called her and I said, “Iris?” And she said, “Yes?” I said, “Well?” And she said, “Not while my mother’s alive!” Then she ended up doing it anyway.”

We’d like to thank our patreon supporters for allowing us to bring you all posts like this one.

- Nick @ Gems
